new_body_evidence.text: The most commonly used technique to estimate the parameters of a data set assuming the Weibull distribution is the maximum likelihood estimation technique (henceforth called the iterative MLE). The problem with this technique is that it returns biased estimators. The exact amount of bias is unknown and depends on the sample size. As a consequence, it is not possible to compare the parameter values obtained from samples of different sizes. As an example, for a very small sample (eight observations), the shape and scale parameters can be underestimated by more than  $40\%$  and  $30\%$ , respectively (these figures were approximated using Monte Carlo simulations described later). Overall, if the three parameters are seen as a vector, the length of the estimated vector is wrong by over  $50\%$ . For medium-sized samples  $(n = 32)$ , the vector is still wrong by over  $10\%$ . Averaging the parameters across multiple participants (assuming they have identical reponse-time distributions) can be used to reduce the variability of the estimates, but this cannot eliminate the biases. Because experiments in psychology rarely have the same sample sizes, this is a major obstacle for cross-experiment comparisons, an obstacle that we wish to eliminate in the present paper.

In the following, we extend the MLE technique by incorporating three weights into the solutions to the maximum likelihood equations. Exact expressions for these weights are given, but being based on the (unknown) population parameters, we instead examine their expected values. In doing so, we will need to move from an iterative MLE technique to a two-step method in which two of the parameters are estimated iteratively and the last one is estimated algebraically. Finally, Monte Carlo simulations will examine the performance of the iterative versus the two-step MLEs, and within the two-step methods, the impact of the weights on the bias of the parameters.

This was confirmed by simulations. Across simulations, we varied the sample size  $n$  (8, 16, 32) and the population shape  $\gamma$  (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5). The scale and shift parameters, being scaling parameters (see Rouder et al., 2005, footnote 3, for a definition), were held constant at  $\{\beta = 100, \alpha = 300\}$ . The shape parameters were chosen such that there are two for which the regular MLE should be both efficient and normally distributed  $(\gamma \geq 2)$ , two for which the regular MLE should work but where the distributions of the estimates are not normal  $(1 \leq \gamma < 2)$ , and the last case  $(\gamma < 1)$  corresponds to a situation for which there should be no consistent estimators (Smith, 1985).

new_body_evidence.text: Now we have a stream of estimation methods available for the three-parameter Weibull distribution, methods that are well researched on the theoretical aspect of the estimation method individually. However, the small sample comparison in terms of bias and root mean squared error (RMSE) of L-moment estimator vis-à-vis other popular estimators is not documented in the literature. We attempt to fill this gap up by comparing the LM estimation method with other methods, namely, MLE, MMLE, LSE, MoE, MMoE, and the MPS. Thereby the main aim of the article becomes developing a guideline of choosing the best estimation method for the three-parameter Weilbull distribution, which we think would be of deep interest to applied statisticians.

To establish the small sample performance of various estimators, we conducted a simulation study. We chose parameter values that were consistent with most of the applications in various fields, including quality control, engineering, actuarial sciences, and finance. The parameter values used in simulations are reported in the simulation design of Table 1. The effect of various shape parameter values on the distribution is depicted in Figure 1. We opted for eight values of the shape parameter, $\beta = 0 . 5$ , 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 3, 4, 6, and 9, to cover the cases where the distribution is positively skewed (for $\beta \leq 3$ , generally in both the engineering and finance cases, see, e.g., Corrado 1996; Corrado and Su 1996; Corrado and Su 1997), and negatively skewed for $\beta \geq 4$ .

We considered $\nu = 9 0$ and kept the scale parameter $\eta$ constant at 100, for consistency. The sample sizes $( n )$ considered are 10, 20, 50, and 100, in order to cover the small, medium, and large sample sizes encountered in real-life data.

In MLE, there is no guarantee that the location parameter, ν, will remain nonnegative (see, e.g., Green et al. 1994; Smith and Naylor 1987). Green et al. (1994) examined profile of the log-likelihood function to investigate why ML yields negative estimates of ν. Smith and Naylor (1987) imposed the constraint of $0 < \nu \leq X _ { 1 : n }$ in their estimation procedure. We imposed the same constraint on $\nu$ for MLE and also for other estimation methods for comparison purposes. We used MoE estimates as starting values for the ML method, and used MLE estimates as starting values for the modified versions of the ML method. For the MPS method we used both MLE and MoE estimates as starting values; the results did not depend on the choice of starting values.

Note. For each of the preceding parameter combinations, we computed the bias and root mean squared errors (RMSE) for sample sizes of ${ \mathrm { ~ n ~ } } = 1 0$ , 20, 50, and 100. The results are based on 5000 simulations.

In simulations, we considered only those cases where ML converged and the sample L-skewness was $\geq - 0 . 1 6 9 9$ . This effectively limits the computations to samples for which all of the competing estimation methods can be used, and provides a fair comparison of the small sample performance of the various estimators.

We initially considered 12 methods of estimation. Of all the methods, LSE, MMoE2, MMoE3, and MMLE3 showed the worst small-sample performance. Thus, we removed these methods from our presentation. The methods (along with the simulation results) reported in Tables 2–9 are MLE, LM, MMLE1, MMLE2, MoE, MMoE1, and MPS. Good estimators have small bias and RMSE. The choice of the estimator in the finite sample largely depends on estimating the shape parameter (β) accurately and precisely (jointly measured by the RMSE). When the RMSE of two methods is close, we preferred the method that had lower bias. Keeping this in view, we analyzed the results. Also, for $\beta < ~ 1$ , we omitted the simulation of the MLE altogether, since the method can not give reliable results in these cases for the reason given in section 3.2. The key findings are as follows:
In this section we apply MLE, LM, MoE, MMLE1, MMLE2, MMoE1, and the MPS estimators to the following two examples. The data are taken from published works.

The attempt is made to use our findings of section 4.2 to get the best estimator of $\beta$ ： (or the true value of $\beta$ ) from real data in Table 10. The competition boils down to just two, MLE and MPS, as others can easily be ruled out due to $\beta$ being expected to be not greater than 2 in these examples. In Example 1, we believe that $\beta$ is less than or equal to 1 and the MPS is the right estimator to use here. The reason is when $\beta \leq 1$ (see Tables 2–4), the LM, MoE, and MMoE1 have overestimated $\beta$ and MLE and MMLE2 underestimated $\beta$ , and MMLE1 estimate is far off true $\beta$ on average. The same pattern follows in this sample (Example 1) if we believe true $\beta$ is less than or equal to 1. Nevertheless, MLE is not the ideal choice when $\beta \leq 1$ as the estimator is inconsistent and inefficient and MLE fails to converge. We can get an idea of it from the $\nu$ estimate, which fails to converge and is replaced by first data observation. Thus, we believe MPS is the right estimation method and that its estimates are more reliable than any others.

For each sample size $( n )$ and the specified values of the parameters (see Table 1), 5000 data sets are generated from the Weibull distribution, as per Eq. (1). From each data set, the estimates of the parameters $( \beta , \eta , \nu )$ are obtained by the methods listed in section 3. For comparing the small sample performance of the estimators, as discussed earlier, we considered bias and the RMSE. We compute the bias of an estimator as the difference between an estimator’s expectation and the true value of the parameter being estimated. Since the bias is the difference between the estimated and true values of the parameter, it does not take the variation in estimates into account, which is measured by the standard deviation of an estimator. If an estimator is biased, then the minimum variance of an estimator does not make it the best estimator. Thus, in such a situation, the RMSE is used to compare the different estimators, rather than using the unbiasedness and minimum variance. The RMSE of an estimator is one way of quantifying the difference between an estimator and the true value of the quantity being estimated. We take the RMSE as the square root of the sum of the variance and the squared bias of an estimator, that is, $\mathrm { R M S E } = \sqrt { \mathrm { V a r } + \mathrm { B i a s } ^ { 2 } }$ , and thus assesses the quality of an estimator in terms of its variation and unbiasedness together. This incorporates both the variance of an estimator and its bias. For an unbiased estimator, the RMSE is simply its standard deviation. The RMSE will only be small when both the variance and the bias of an estimator are small.

In simulations, we considered only those cases where ML converged and the sample L-skewness was $\geq - 0 . 1 6 9 9$ . This effectively limits the computations to samples for which all of the competing estimation methods can be used, and provides a fair comparison of the small sample performance of the various estimators.

new_body_evidence.text: We carry out a Monte Carlo simulation study to evaluate the performance of the proposed estimators. The proposed estimators, termed LSPFs, which is the abbreviation for location and scale parameters free maximum likelihood estimators, are compared with the BL estimators (BLEs) proposed by Hall and Wang (2005), and the weighted maximum likelihood estimators (w-MLEs) proposed by Cousineau (2009b). Hall and Wang (2005) concluded from their simulation study that the BL method in general outperforms the MPS method and the CL method, while (Cousineau, 2009a) reported from an empirical study that the w-ML method in general outperforms the ML and MPS methods as well as the method of moments and therefore the comparison of the proposed LSPFs with BLEs and w-MLEs seems appropriate and adequate.

In the simulation study, the values ofthe shape parameter $\beta$ are selected as 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0. For the location and scale parameters. we take $\gamma = 0$ and $\alpha = 1$ . new_body_evidence.text: This section presents an assessment of PITE with ρ =0.32, 0.42, 0.68, 1.00, compared to MLE, WMLE, MPSE, and MOM through a Monte Carlo simulation. The simulations are executed using R statistical software version 4.4.131. Note that the R commands for the other estimators used in this study are accessible in the ForestFit package32.

Step 1. Generate random samples from a Weibull distribution with sample sizes of n = 50, 100, and 500. The shape parameter θ varies among 2, 4, or 6, with the scale parameter β and the location parameter γ are fixed at 3 and at 1, respectively, throughout the simulation study.

Step 2. Introduce outliers by replacing some random observations. These outliers are generated from another Weibull distribution with the same shape and location parameters but with the scale parameter adjusted by a factor ω = 5 for outliers. The outliers are added in fixed proportions ε = 2%, 4%, 6%, 8%.
Step 3. Estimate the parameters θ, β, and γ using PITE (ρ = 0.32, 0.42, 0.68, 1.00), MLE, WMLE, MPSE, and MOM.
Step 4. Repeat steps 1–3 for a total of 5,000 iterations.

Fig. 4. RMSE values for different estimation methods under varying levels of contamination.
